caps.text: Engineers at Anthropic no longer read every line of code.
Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code.
Yet from June to September, merged PRs more than doubled,
while the share that got reverted fell over 40 percent.
Fewer human eyes. So why is it more stable?
That's from the Claude Code team's October post. Let's take it apart.
First, the pressure. Anthropic's monorepo went from about 2,500 merges a day in May to over 30,000 in September.
Claude Code has its own repo, under a lot of pressure too.
At that speed, line-by-line human review is close to impossible.
But they didn't remove review. They moved most of the reading to machines.
Code review does two jobs: catch problems before they ship, and spread understanding of the code.
They argue that "did a human read it?" is an imprecise proxy.
The real question: what could go wrong, and which check, automated or human, should catch it?
And review is no longer a gate at the end of the road. It runs all the time, like spellcheck.
The scarce resource is human time and attention.
It has two sides: time reviewing, and time fixing what bad code breaks. Save one, lose the other, and you saved nothing.
So the goal: most PRs merge with at most one human, who can be the author, with revert and incident rates as the guardrail.
Their answer: not one gate, but six layers of checks, with a rollback net underneath.
Every layer misses something. Few problems get through all of them.
Layer one, before the PR: Claude runs the checks and shows the output, not just "done."
Then a subagent with fresh context reviews the diff.
Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, calls verification probably the most important thing,
and estimates it makes results two to three times better.
When the same comment keeps coming up, they fix it at the source: a skill, a lint rule, or CLAUDE.md and REVIEW.md.
Good REVIEW.md files are short and say what failure looks like. For docs: "it lies."
Layer two: every PR gets a Claude review. Agents hunt for bugs, others vote on each finding, and only agreed ones are posted.
Survivors are tagged Important, Nit or Pre-existing, so an old bug isn't blamed on the author. Every finding must be answered.
At launch, internal PRs getting substantive comments went from 16 to 54 percent.
Layer three, security review. Layer four, required CI. Any open finding, or anything red, blocks the merge.
And every PR says how it was tested, and how to undo it.
Layer five: human approval scaled by risk. Docs: zero people. Ordinary changes: one. The riskiest code: two.
The change sets the tier, not the author, and a classifier picks it. Only trusted authors get the lighter paths.
An agent's approval never counts as a human's,
and whoever directed the agent counts as a reviewer, as if they had typed it themselves.
Layer six: a merge queue re-checks against the latest main. New features ship behind a flag, to employees first, then gradually.
The net at the bottom: flags turn off without a deploy, and most mistakes are undone in minutes.
As one colleague put it: slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you do less of everything.
They'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing.
Is the reviewer any good? Every incident becomes an exam question, and the reviewer takes the exam daily.
Change its prompts, tools or model, and the change stays only if the score goes up.
Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person waves off a nit. An agent fixes it, and that is another round.
The wildest case: an AI author and an AI reviewer took one PR through more than fifty rounds overnight, until its author stopped it.
Git blame showed about 59 percent of what the reviewer kept flagging had been there since its first pass.
It was rarely finding new bugs, just a few more old ones each round.
So they changed the rules. After three rounds, the author steps back and rethinks. After the first few passes, review only the new diff.
Flag the whole class of bug. Never repeat a finding.
The result: PRs passing after one round went from 65 to 78 percent.
PRs needing five or more rounds fell from 8.9 to 1.5 percent.
Mean reviews to pass: from 2.08 down to 1.32.
So what do people do? Pulling a senior engineer away to catch a routine mistake costs too much.
People keep what machines are bad at: whether to build it, risky code, architecture others will copy, reading the evidence,
and owning the outcome.
How does anyone learn the code? They ask Claude for an explainer of exactly that slice.
A one-line copy change teaches you almost nothing. An explainer teaches you a lot.
The team norm: you land it, you own it.
Changes are small and reversible, bigger risk gets more checks, and incident reviews look at the system, not the person.
Want to try it? A short CLAUDE.md and REVIEW.md, AI and security review,
risk-tiered approval, capped review rounds, a merge queue, flags, one-step rollback, and incidents turned into an eval.
They say the line for what can merge on automated checks alone keeps moving.
Review didn't disappear. It moved from 'a human read it' to 'a human owns it.'
And your team? Who reviews your code now?
